Slow
SLOH
adj.
From Old English slaw, sluggish, dull. Webster 1828: moving a small distance in a long time; not ready; not prompt; dull; inactive. In Scripture it is one of the great words of the divine character — slow to anger — and one of the sharpest words of rebuke — slow of heart to believe.

Biblical Definition

Slow is used of God with reverence and of men with reproach. When the LORD proclaimed His name to Moses in the cleft of the rock, the second attribute after mercy was longsuffering, and the phrase that carries it through the Old Testament is slow to anger: The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy (Psalm 103:8). Nehemiah’s great prayer of confession says the same of a God dealing with a people who had appointed a captain to return to Egypt: thou art a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and forsookest them not (Nehemiah 9:17). God’s slowness here is not weakness or indifference; it is deliberate forbearance while judgment is deserved, and Peter says the same thing of the delay of the second advent — the Lord is not slack concerning his promise… but is longsuffering to us-ward. James then commands the imitation of it in the most practical terms in the epistle: let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19). And the risen Christ uses the word as a rebuke on the Emmaus road: O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken (Luke 24:25).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SLOW as moving a small distance in a long time; not swift; not ready; not prompt or quick; dull; inactive; tardy. He also gives the sense of being late or behindhand, which is exactly what 2 Peter 3:9 denies of God.

expand to see more

SLOW, a. — Moving a small distance in a long time; not swift; not quick in motion.

Not ready; not prompt or quick; as slow of speech, slow to anger.

Dull; inactive; tardy; late; behind in time.

Not hasty; acting with deliberation; a sense in which slowness is a virtue and not a defect.

The last sense is the biblical one when the word is used of God: deliberate forbearance, not tardiness.

Key Scripture

Psalm 103:8 — "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy."

Nehemiah 9:17 — "And refused to obey, neither were mindful of thy wonders that thou didst among them; but hardened their necks, and in their rebellion appointed a captain to return to their bondage: but thou art a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and forsookest them not."

James 1:19 — "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:"

Luke 24:25 — "Then he said unto them, O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken:"

Exodus 34:6 — "And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth,"

Modern Corruption

God’s slowness to anger is regularly heard as mildness — a God who does not really get angry — when Scripture means a God whose anger is real, deserved, and deliberately delayed.

expand to see more

The Hebrew behind slow to anger is literally long of nostrils, a figure for a long fuse; the anger is presumed and its arrival is postponed. Exodus 34, the very proclamation of mercy and grace and longsuffering, ends by saying that He will by no means clear the guilty. Both clauses are the same self-revelation. A God who is slow to anger is not a God incapable of it, and a mercy that has no wrath behind it is not mercy but indifference. This matters because the modern instinct is to purchase divine kindness by denying divine judgment, and the trade always fails: a God who cannot be provoked cannot be reconciled either, and the cross becomes unintelligible.

James turns the attribute into a command and puts it where it does the most work. Swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath is written to a scattered church with real grievances, and the order is deliberate: listening first, speech delayed, anger delayed longest. He adds the reason, for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God, which forecloses the standard defence that one is angry on God’s behalf. And Luke 24:25 supplies the one slowness Christ rebukes. Slow to speak is a virtue; slow of heart to believe what the prophets have spoken is folly, and He cured it not by comfort but by expounding in all the scriptures the things concerning Himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew erek appayim, long of nostrils, that is slow to anger; Greek bradus (G1021), slow, in James 1:19 and Luke 24:25.

expand to see more

Hebrew erek (H750) — long, patient; joined to aph, the nostril, for the idiom slow to anger.

Hebrew aph (H639) — the nose or nostril, and by extension anger, from the flaring of the nostrils.

Greek bradus (G1021) — slow, dull; slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19).

Greek braduno (G1019) — to be slow, to delay; the Lord is not slack concerning his promise (2 Peter 3:9) uses the related bradun.

Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, long-tempered; the New Testament equivalent of the Hebrew idiom.

Usage

"Slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy (Psalm 103:8) — deliberate forbearance, not mildness."

"Swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19) — the attribute turned into a command."

"O fools, and slow of heart to believe (Luke 24:25) — the one slowness Christ rebukes."
